text.text:
### Prerequisites

In this text, we continue studying division by three. Therefore, we recommend reading the previous text, which introduces the topic (<htcite0>).

Once you have read it, you are ready to continue: here we will follow the idea of the atom from its first philosophical guess all the way to modern particle physics, and we will notice again and again how often nature organizes itself in groups of three.

### Introduction

In this text, we develop the idea that division reveals something inherent in nature: a process of redistribution without loss. When matter is divided, it does not disappear — it is conserved, as concluded by Antoine Lavoisier (<htcite0>; <htcite1>).

Think about it: if you break a bar of chocolate into squares, no chocolate is lost. The same amount is still there; it has only been rearranged into smaller pieces.

However, division should not be seen merely as something that separates. In many cases, it is necessary to define groups through divisions before building something: we first sort the bricks into piles or cut the cloth into pattern pieces, and only then do we begin to build. This leads us to the following reflection:

Reflection 1: Dividing to Multiply

Is it easier to build something by moving huge, heavy pieces that you can’t carry?

Or is it simpler to build something using pieces that you can carry?

### First Idea

In the previous text (<htcite0>), when revisiting the example of the divided leaf, we noticed that there is at least one more element: the center — the point where the two halves meet — which is often ignored because our focus tends to be on the edges.

Let’s perform a few more divisions using only one half of the leaf. The other half can wait: half a leaf is already more than enough pieces for us to work with.

Practice 1: Cutting...

Purpose: to feel by hand how quickly the number of pieces grows as you keep dividing.

1. Take a sheet of paper and cut it into pieces. It’s not necessary to follow the pattern shown in Table 1.

2. Keep cutting until you get tired or until you wish to stop.

Before you stop, count the pieces: the number grows much faster than you probably expect.

Shredded leaf

Table 1: Visual representation of a leaf cut into 100 pieces.

#### The Maximum Possible

In the case of *History Tracers*, we decided to stop at 100 small pieces, so that creating the table does not use too many computer resources.

When you did the practice, you probably also stopped for some reason — tired hands, pieces too small to hold, or paper that simply fell apart.

Both situations share the same pattern: at some point, our tools set a limit on how far we can divide. This brings us to a question about possible limits:

Reflection 2: The Smallest

If, for some reason, we can no longer divide a leaf because of our own nature, does that mean the leaf cannot be divided any further?

#### The First Idea

The first ideas suggesting that nature might contain something indivisible date back thousands of years. The first to propose this hypothesis is believed to have been Democritus, who was born around <htdate0>.

The very word **atom** comes from a Greek word meaning “uncuttable”: the smallest piece, beyond which nothing can be divided.

According to his model of indivisible matter, the universe was composed of four fundamental elements: earth, water, air, and fire (<htcite0>).

Democritus’ initial idea was based on several important points (<htcite1>):
- Atoms would exist in an “infinite number.” It is important to note that infinity is not a number, but something greater than any quantity (<htcite2>). Therefore, it would be more accurate to say that the number of atoms **tends toward infinity** (<htcite3>).
- Atoms would have different sizes.
- They would be solid.
- There would be no spaces between them.

This model, containing only four elements and completely solid atoms, is represented in **Figure 1**. Keep it in mind: more than two thousand years later, scientists would finally test it in the laboratory.
Figure 1: Philosophical model of the atom. © History Tracers.

### Classical Atomic Models

The deep study of atoms and the understanding of how the Universe is formed took millennia to develop. From this point on, we will follow four scientists in turn, each one testing and improving the model left by the previous one: Dalton, Thomson, Rutherford and Chadwick.

The first researcher we refer to is John Dalton (Book 1). In his studies, Dalton concluded that matter is made up of small particles called atoms. In addition, by studying fluids, he inferred properties such as the weight of elements (<htcite0>).
Book 1: Page 73 of John Dalton’s work.

Another important advance in understanding atoms was made by J. J. Thomson, who, through experiments, discovered that atoms contain subatomic charged particles. This particle is known as the electron (<htcite0>). In other words, the atom — believed to be indivisible since the time of Democritus — could be split after all.

Thomson also proposed a theory to explain why charged particles are deflected when passing through small amounts of matter — a theory later confirmed by Ernest Rutherford’s experiments. According to the proposed model, the atom consists of electrons orbiting a positively charged sphere concentrated at the center (<htcite1>). Picture a cake with little pieces of fruit scattered through it: the body of the cake is the positively charged sphere, and the pieces of fruit are the electrons.

Practice 2: Building Rutherford’s Model

Purpose: to build by hand the model Rutherford proposed, so that you can picture his experiment when we describe it below.

We will use sheets of paper to recreate Graph 1.

1. Take three sheets of the same size.

2. Paint them in different colors.

3. Choose one sheet and crumple it into a ball. It will represent the nucleus of the atom.

4. Take another sheet, cut it into small equal pieces, and crumple them. Place them around the first, larger ball — these will represent the electrons.

5. Repeat step 4 with the remaining sheet, but this time gently throw the small balls so that they travel along paths A, B and C of the graph. They will represent the alpha particles fired at the foil.
Graph 1: Representation of the Rutherford model. Paths A go straight through, path B bounces back, and path C is deflected.
text.imgdesc: Representation of Rutherford's atom, which features a large positive nucleus and small, negatively charged electrons around it.

text.text:
The Rutherford atomic model shows that the atom is not solid, but divided into two regions (<htcite0>): a dense, positively charged nucleus — made of tiny particles called protons — and an outer region where the negatively charged electrons are located.

Rutherford reached this conclusion by firing alpha particles (the small balls from step 5 of Practice 2) at a gold foil. Observing the paths of these particles, he noticed that they could be deflected in different directions, indicating that atoms contain empty internal spaces (<htcite1>; <htcite2>). It is like throwing balls at a thick hedge: most of them fly straight through the gaps, while a few hit a branch and bounce back. Had the atom been completely solid, every single particle would have bounced back.

Reflection 3: Science Is Practice

The model developed by Democritus was a correct idea, but it was never tested in his time. For this reason, we cannot say he was truly doing science.

When J. J. Thomson proposed a model and Ernest Rutherford tested it, improving our understanding, we saw science in action — theory being built through practice and experimentation.

Have you ever heard the mistaken idea that science has no practical side?

Although this atomic model with two regions explained some observations, it could not account for all the measurements made. In this context, in <htdate0>, James Chadwick conducted new experiments that demonstrated that, in addition to the protons in the nucleus and the electrons around it, there was another particle in the nucleus of the atom — a particle with no electric charge, which became known as the neutron (<htcite0>).

With the neutron discovered, the atom now had its three familiar particles: protons, neutrons and electrons.

### Deepening Our Knowledge

As we advance in our studies, new experiments have been carried out, and our understanding of atoms has been continuously updated. A model is never the last word: every experiment either supports it or forces it to change.

In addition to experiments such as those by James Chadwick, who fired different particles at one another (<htcite0>), it is also possible to accelerate identical particles toward each other to gain an even deeper understanding of matter and energy. This is the operating principle behind particle accelerators, such as the one at CERN: machines that push particles to almost the speed of light and then crash them together, so that scientists can study the fragments. Among the discoveries made through these experiments is the confirmation of the existence of the Higgs boson, proposed in <htdate0> and confirmed in <htdate1> — the particle that gives other particles their mass (<htcite1>; <htcite2>).

Particle accelerators have also shown that protons and neutrons are not indivisible, meaning that an atom should not be understood simply as consisting of protons, electrons, and neutrons.

In <htdate2>, two scientists proposed the existence of particles that, if present within protons and neutrons — also known as hadrons — could explain certain experimental observations. Four years later, in <htdate3>, these internal particles, called quarks, were detected, helping us to further understand the structure of the universe (<htcite3>; <htcite4>).

With these discoveries, we moved from an initial understanding that atoms were composed of three fundamental particles (protons, electrons, and neutrons) to recognizing that protons and neutrons are each made up of **three quarks**, and that together they form the atomic nucleus. Orbiting around this nucleus are the electrons.

So the group of three appears again at every level: three kinds of particle in the atom, and three quarks inside each proton and each neutron.

These quarks were the first particles to appear in the universe, when it was less than three minutes old, as shown in Figure 3 (<htcite0>):
Figure 3: Planck, History of the Universe. ©ESA – C. Carreau ().

Since this text focuses on groups and divisions of three, we will, for now, limit ourselves to these explanations about the atom. In future texts, we will continue exploring the structure of matter and what we understand about the evolution of the universe.

### Conclusion

In this text, we observed how matter can be grouped or divided into sets of three, focusing on the evolution of our understanding of the atoms that make up matter. We began with the philosophical idea, moved on to experiments conducted in the 19th century (according to the Gregorian calendar), and finally examined the relationship between hypotheses and practices that continuously update our understanding of nature — showing that science is a dynamic process.

Three ideas are worth taking with you:
- Matter is conserved when it is divided: the pieces change, the total does not.
- No model is final; each one is tested and improved by the next experiment.
- Groups of three keep appearing: three particles in the atom, and three quarks in each proton and neutron.

There is still much to explore regarding these divisions. In upcoming texts, we will begin studying groups of four found in the universe and, consequently, in our daily lives.

exercise_v2.question: Is Democritus’s first idea of the atom the same as the one we have today?
exercise_v2.additionalInfo: The atom as we understand it today is very different from Democritus’s concept. This understanding has been refined through various studies and experiments carried out over the past centuries.

exercise_v2.question: Does the nucleus of the atom contain only protons and neutrons?
exercise_v2.additionalInfo: For a time, this was the prevailing belief. However, experiments have shown that hadrons (protons and neutrons) are made up of smaller particles — one of which, the quark, is presented in this text.

exercise_v2.question: Science has no experiments; it consists of unquestionable beliefs. Is this statement correct?
exercise_v2.additionalInfo: A piece of knowledge is only recognized as a scientific theory when it can be tested and verified. No matter how beautiful or profound a theoretical idea may be, it cannot be considered science if it cannot be observed or measured.
